body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"A decision aid for dental pain in general practice and antibiotic prescribing: a cluster randomised trial","authors":"Halvorsen-Mbatha J, Price-Okonkwo L, Varga-Tennant S","year":2020,"venue":"Primary Care Prescribing Research","doi":"10.5555/pcpr.2020.0233","providerType":"Randomized Controlled Trial","abstract":"We randomly allocated 24 general practices to a one-page decision aid for dental pain with access to urgent dental advice, or to usual care, for 12 months. Among 4,310 dental pain consultations, antibiotic prescribing fell from 61 to 38 percent in intervention practices and from 60 to 55 percent in control practices. Hospital admissions for dental infection within 14 days were 0.4 percent in intervention practices and 0.5 percent in control practices. Repeat consultations for the same problem did not increase. The intracluster correlation for prescribing was 0.06. Practices were self-selected and had better access to dentists than average."},{"title":"Antibiotics for toothache caused by pulpitis or apical periodontitis in adults: a systematic review of placebo-controlled comparisons","authors":"Nakamura-Ellis F, Oduya-Grant H","year":2018,"venue":"Oral Health Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/ohr.2018.0077","providerType":"systematic review","abstract":"We searched four databases for placebo-controlled comparisons of systemic antibiotics for adults with toothache from irreversible pulpitis or acute apical periodontitis. Six small trials with 412 participants were included. When dental treatment was also provided, antibiotics did not reduce pain or swelling compared with placebo at 24 or 72 hours. No trial studied people who could not obtain dental treatment. Adverse effects were more common with antibiotics. Certainty was low because of small samples and imprecision. The review supports reserving antibiotics for spreading infection or systemic signs."},{"title":"Same-day dental telephone triage for people presenting to general practice with toothache: first-year service data","authors":"Community Dental Service Development Team","year":null,"venue":"Dental public health conference abstracts","providerType":"conference abstract","abstract":"A community dental service ran a same-day telephone triage line for patients referred by general practices with toothache. In its first year the line took 1,140 calls. Dental nurses booked 62 percent of callers for urgent dental care within 48 hours and gave self-care and analgesia advice to 29 percent. Antibiotics were advised for 9 percent, mostly for facial swelling or fever. The abstract does not state the year of the service data, the number of practices involved or what happened to patients who were not booked. No comparison with prescribing before the line opened is reported."},{"title":"Management of acute dental problems for prescribers who are not dentists","authors":"Oral Health Advisory Panel","year":null,"venue":"Clinical guidance leaflet series","providerType":"guidance leaflet","abstract":"This guidance leaflet for doctors, nurses and pharmacists covers toothache, dental abscess, ulcers and dental trauma. For toothache without swelling it recommends analgesia with paracetamol or ibuprofen and referral for dental treatment. Antibiotics are recommended only for spreading infection, systemic signs such as fever, or when urgent dental treatment cannot be obtained and infection is present. Red flags for same-day hospital referral include difficulty swallowing, trismus and swelling extending to the eye or neck. The leaflet gives no publication date, and its evidence sources are not listed."},{"title":"Adults without a regular dentist and dental consultations in general practice: a population analysis","authors":"Abara-Lindqvist P, Moreno-Achterberg C","year":2022,"venue":"Journal of Primary Care Equity","doi":"10.5555/jpce.2022.0149","providerType":"cross-sectional study","abstract":"We linked a population survey of adults to practice consultation data in one region. In the most deprived fifth of neighbourhoods, 38 percent of adults had no regular dentist, compared with 17 percent in the least deprived fifth. Adults without a regular dentist were three times as likely to consult a general practitioner for dental pain in a year. Among these consultations, antibiotic prescribing was more common where the nearest dental practice accepting new patients was more than 10 kilometres away. The survey response rate was 46 percent."},{"title":"Why general practitioners prescribe antibiotics for toothache: an interview study","authors":"Whitfield-Oyelaran R, Castellanos-Nair D","year":2024,"venue":"Northgate Primary Care Qualitative Research","doi":"10.5555/npcqr.2024.0036","providerType":"qualitative research","abstract":"We interviewed 21 general practitioners about consultations for dental pain. Most described prescribing antibiotics because patients could not get dental care, because they feared missing a spreading infection, or because patients expected a prescription after waiting to be seen. Several said they lacked confidence in examining the mouth. Doctors wanted a direct route to same-day dental advice and a short decision aid that fitted into a ten-minute consultation. Some worried that declining antibiotics would lead patients to attend emergency departments instead."},{"title":"Emergency department attendances for dental infection after changes in access to dental care","authors":"Keane-Obafemi T, Sundberg-Rao M","year":2016,"venue":"Emergency Dental Epidemiology","doi":"10.5555/ede.2016.0012","providerType":"observational study","abstract":"We examined emergency department attendances for dental abscess and facial swelling over three years in which the number of dental practices accepting new adult patients fell. Attendances rose by 24 percent over the period. Admissions for spreading dental infection remained rare at about 0.3 per 10,000 adults per year but were concentrated in adults without a regular dentist. Most attenders had seen a general practitioner or pharmacist in the week before. The analysis could not link attendances to earlier antibiotic prescriptions."}]}
